summary: Arabic has two basic verb forms, the perfect (past, with endings: أَكَلْتُ “I ate”) and the imperfect, which is the present: يَأْكُلُ “he eats, he is eating”. The present is built with a prefix that shows the person — ʾa- (I), ta- (you; she), ya- (he; they), na- (we) — and, for some persons, an ending: -īna (you, one woman), -ūna (you / they, men or mixed), -na (women only). So one word holds the person, the gender and the number: تَطْبُخِينَ = “you (a woman) cook”, and the pronoun is normally left out. Dictionaries list a verb by its past “he” form (أَكَلَ, “he ate”) — there is no infinitive — so learn each verb with its present: أَكَلَ / يَأْكُلُ, شَرِبَ / يَشْرَبُ, طَبَخَ / يَطْبُخُ. The vowel before the last root letter (u, a or i) must be learned with each simple verb; derived verbs have fixed patterns: أَرَادَ → يُرِيدُ, أَحَبَّ → يُحِبُّ (u in the prefix), اِشْتَرَى → يَشْتَرِي. One form covers “I eat”, “I am eating” and, from context, “I will eat”. Arabic also has forms for two people (the dual: يَأْكُلَانِ “they two eat”); they come later.

blocks.caption: A regular (sound) verb: طَبَخَ / يَطْبُخُ “to cook”. The same prefixes and endings come back in every verb.

blocks.title: Four prefixes, three endings.
blocks.text: Prefix: أَ I · تَ you, she · يَ he, they · نَ we. Ending: -u in most persons; -īna for “you” to one woman; -ūna for “you” and “they” (men or mixed groups); -na for women only. تَطْبُخُ — تَطْبُخِينَ — تَطْبُخُونَ — تَطْبُخْنَ.

blocks.caption: Form I verbs: the stem vowel is u in يَأْكُلُ and يَطْبُخُ, a in يَشْرَبُ. “I eat” is آكُلُ: the hamza of the prefix and the hamza of the root merge into آ.

head: who
أَرَادَ (want)
أَحَبَّ (like)
اِشْتَرَى (buy)
blocks.caption: Derived verbs: form IV أَرَادَ and أَحَبَّ take u in the prefix (أُرِيدُ، يُحِبُّ); form VIII اِشْتَرَى keeps a (يَشْتَرِي) and ends in -ī. Before -na the long ī of يُرِيدُ shortens (تُرِدْنَ) and the doubled b of يُحِبُّ splits (تُحْبِبْنَ).

blocks.title: تَـ is two persons.
blocks.text: تَشْرَبُ means “you (a man) drink” and “she drinks”; تَشْتَرِينَ means “you (a woman) buy” and also “you (women) buy”. The context — or a pronoun — tells you who.

blocks.title: No pronoun needed.
blocks.text: أَشْرَبُ الشَّايَ = I drink tea. Add the pronoun only to stress it: أَنَا أَشْرَبُ الشَّايَ، وَهُوَ يَشْرَبُ الْقَهْوَةَ (I drink tea, and he drinks coffee).

items.title: Noun first
points: the verb agrees fully: singular, plural, gender

items.title: Verb first (the classic order)
points: the verb stays singular before a noun subject; only the gender shows: تَأْكُلُ الْبِنْتُ

blocks.text: Both orders are correct. In this course the sentences put the noun first, as in everyday writing; the verb-first versions are accepted as answers.

blocks.title: One present for three English tenses.
blocks.text: آكُلُ = I eat / I am eating / (often) I will eat. The future can be marked with سَـ or سَوْفَ (سَآكُلُ, “I will eat”) — later. To negate the present put لَا before it (lesson 8): لَا آكُلُ.

For you: Greek, Russian and German also show the person in the verb (τρώω, ем, ich esse) — Arabic does it mostly at the front of the verb. Turkish piles endings at the back (yiyorum); Arabic puts most of the information in the prefix.

askYourself: Who does it? I → أَ, we → نَ, he / they → يَ, you / she → تَ.
Is it “you” to one woman? → -īna (تَشْرَبِينَ). “You” or “they” for men or a mixed group? → -ūna (تَشْرَبُونَ). Women only? → -na (تَشْرَبْنَ، يَشْرَبْنَ).
Which vowel does this verb have before its last root letter in the present (يَأْكُلُ u, يَشْرَبُ a, يَطْبُخُ u)? I take it from the verb’s present form, not from the past.
Is it a form IV verb (أَرَادَ، أَحَبَّ)? → u in the prefix: أُرِيدُ، يُحِبُّ.
Is the subject a noun? Noun first → full agreement (الْأَطْفَالُ يُرِيدُونَ); verb first → the verb stays singular (يُرِيدُ الْأَطْفَالُ).
Do I need the pronoun? Only for contrast or emphasis.

traps: The citation form is the past “he” form: أَكَلَ means “he ate”, not “to eat”. The present is يَأْكُلُ.
Do not carry the past vowel into the present: شَرِبَ → يَشْرَبُ (not *يَشْرِبُ), أَكَلَ → يَأْكُلُ.
I eat = آكُلُ (ʾākulu), not *أَأْكُلُ: two hamzas merge into آ.
Form IV verbs take u in the prefix: أُحِبُّ، أُرِيدُ — not *أَحِبُّ، *أَرِيدُ.
Verb before a plural noun subject stays singular: يَشْرَبُ الطُّلَّابُ — but الطُّلَّابُ يَشْرَبُونَ.
تَشْتَرِينَ is both “you (one woman) buy” and “you (women) buy” — read the context.

quiz.why: na- is “we”; ʾa- is “I”, ya- “he”, ta-…-ūna “you (pl)”.

quiz.q: “You (to a woman) want …” — which form of أَرَادَ?
quiz.why: ta- … -īna is “you” to one woman; تُرِيدُ is “you (a man)” or “she”.
A form IV verb: u in the prefix. أَحَبَّ is the past “he liked”.

quiz.q: What does the dictionary form أَكَلَ mean?
quiz.why: Arabic has no infinitive; verbs are listed by the past “he” form.

quiz.q: “The students drink juice”, verb first: which is correct?
quiz.why: Before its noun subject the verb stays singular; noun first it would be الطُّلَّابُ يَشْرَبُونَ.
ya- … -na is “they (women only)”; ta- … -na is “you (women only)”.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew’s present is a participle that changes by gender and number, not by person (אוֹכֵל، אוֹכֶלֶת، אוֹכְלִים، אוֹכְלוֹת) — so it needs the pronoun; Arabic marks the person with a prefix (أَ، تَ، يَ، نَ). The Hebrew future, though, is the twin of the Arabic present (יֹאכַל — يَأْكُلُ).
German conjugates with endings (ich esse, du isst, er isst) and always says the pronoun; Arabic uses prefixes and drops the pronoun.
Chinese verbs never change: 我吃, 你吃, 他吃 — the person is only in the pronoun, the time in words like 现在 or in particles.
The prefix vowel and the stem vowel are part of the verb’s pattern: yafʿalu (يَشْرَبُ), yafʿulu (يَأْكُلُ), yufʿilu (يُرِيدُ).
